title: Evolution and Its Evidence
bigQuestion: What evidence shows that living things change over time, and what forces drive that change?

story.title: The Fish With a Neck
story.kicker: Three scientists used a geology map to predict where a missing fossil should be, then went to the Arctic and found it.
paragraphs: Fish do not have necks. Their skulls are bolted to their shoulders by a row of bones, so a fish turns its whole body to look sideways. Land animals with four limbs, from frogs to people, have a gap there, and can swing the head alone. Fossils show that fish came first and four-limbed animals came later. If that is true, then somewhere in the rocks there should be a creature in between: part fish, part land animal, with a neck.

In the late 1990s, Neil Shubin, Ted Daeschler and Farish Jenkins decided to look for it on purpose. They reasoned like detectives. The first four-limbed animals appear in rocks about 365 million years old. Fish with strong, lobed fins appear in rocks about 385 million years old. So the in-between creature should lie in rocks from about 375 million years ago, laid down by shallow fresh water, and those rocks should be exposed at the surface where no one had dug before.

A geology textbook had a map of exactly such rocks on Ellesmere Island, in the far north of Canada, about 1,000 kilometers from the North Pole. The team went in 1999. They found almost nothing. They went back in 2000, 2002 and 2004. Summers there are short and cold, and polar bears are a real danger. In July 2004 a crew member noticed the snout of a flat-headed animal sticking out of a cliff.

The fossil was a fish, with scales and fins and gills. But its head was flat like a crocodile's, with eyes on top. It had ribs sturdy enough to hold up a body. Inside its front fin were bones that matched a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist. And its skull was free of the shoulder bones. It had a neck. The team named it Tiktaalik, from an Inuktitut word for a large freshwater fish, and published it in 2006.

Tiktaalik was not a guess that got lucky. It was a prediction: this kind of animal, in rocks of this age, in this kind of place. The prediction came true. That is what makes a scientific idea strong. Evolution had said what should be found and where, decades before anyone had found it. This chapter is about the evidence that lets scientists make predictions like that.
story.think: The team predicted the age and setting of a fossil before finding it. Why does a prediction that comes true count as stronger evidence than a lucky find?

lessons.title: Fossils and Deep Time
lessons.mainIdea: Rock layers and radioactive dating let scientists put fossils in order and show that life has changed over billions of years.
reading: In 1669 the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno pointed out something that now seems obvious. Layers of sediment settle one on top of another, so in undisturbed rock, deeper layers are older. Walk down into a canyon and you walk back in time. The *fossils* in each layer, the preserved remains or traces of living things, give a snapshot of life at that time.

Steno's rule gives the order but not the age in years. That came in the twentieth century, when scientists learned to use *radioactive decay* as a clock. Some atoms break down at a steady rate that nothing speeds up or slows down. Measure how much of the original element is left in a volcanic rock layer, and you can compute when it formed. Fossils between two dated layers are bracketed in time. By this method, the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and the oldest known fossils are microbes about 3.5 billion years old.

The record tells a consistent story. Simple single-celled life appears first. Animals with hard parts show up about 540 million years ago. Fish come before amphibians, amphibians before reptiles, reptiles before mammals and birds. No one has ever found a rabbit in rocks from the age of trilobites. And where the record is good, it shows *transitional forms* like Tiktaalik, and like Archaeopteryx, a feathered animal with teeth and a bony tail, found in Germany in 1861.

Illinois has its own window on deep time. The Mazon Creek beds near Braidwood preserve soft-bodied animals and plants from about 309 million years ago, when this region was a warm coastal swamp. The state fossil, the Tully monster, comes from these beds and is so strange that scientists still argue about what group it belongs to.

words.d: the preserved remains, imprint or trace of a living thing from the past
the steady breakdown of certain atoms, used as a clock for dating rocks
a fossil that shows features of both an older group and a newer group

look.title: A Timeline in the Rocks
look.cite: USGS and standard geological references, rounded
look.prompt: If Earth's whole history were one 24-hour day, roughly when would animals with hard parts appear? When would humans?

check.q: In undisturbed layers of rock, the oldest fossils are found:
check.why: Layers pile up over time, so the deepest were laid down first.

check.q: How do scientists find the age of a rock layer in years?
choices: By counting the fossils in it
By measuring the steady decay of radioactive atoms
By comparing it to the Bible's timeline
check.why: Radioactive atoms decay at a fixed rate. The amount left acts as a clock.

check.q: What would count as evidence against the fossil record's story?
choices: A fossil with features of two groups
A microbe fossil 3.5 billion years old
A fish fossil older than the first amphibian
A mammal fossil in rocks older than any fish
check.why: Mammals appear late. Finding one before any fish would break the observed order.

lessons.title: Same Bones, Different Jobs
lessons.mainIdea: Living things share body plans, leftover structures and early stages of development that make sense only if they descend from common ancestors.
reading: Lay out the front limbs of a human, a cat, a whale and a bat. A human arm is for grasping, a cat's leg for running, a whale's flipper for swimming and a bat's wing for flying. Yet all four have the same bones in the same order: one upper bone, two lower bones, a cluster of wrist bones, then the finger bones. The whale's flipper even has finger bones inside it. These are *homologous structures*: same plan, different job. The simplest explanation is that all four inherited the plan from one ancestor.

Compare this to a bird's wing and a butterfly's wing. Both are for flying, but one is built of bone and feathers and the other of thin membrane held by veins. They look alike only on the outside. These are *analogous structures*: same job, different plan. They evolved separately. Homology points to shared ancestry; analogy points to shared problems.

Some structures have no job at all. Whales have small pelvic bones buried in muscle, far from any leg. Some snakes have tiny hind-limb bones. Humans have a tailbone made of fused vertebrae and, in some people, a small muscle that in other mammals moves the ears. These *vestigial structures* are leftovers, shrunken but not gone, from ancestors that used them.

Early development tells the same story. Embryos of fish, chickens, and humans all pass through a stage with a tail and a row of pouches in the neck. In fish the pouches become gills. In humans they become parts of the jaw, ear and throat. A word of caution: the nineteenth-century biologist Ernst Haeckel drew these embryos to look more alike than they are, and his drawings were used in textbooks for a century. The real photos still show the shared stages. The exaggeration was the problem, not the evidence.

words.d: body parts in different species that share the same plan because of a common ancestor
body parts that do the same job but evolved separately from different plans
a shrunken, leftover body part that had a use in an ancestor

look.title: The Flipper's Fingers
look.text: An X-ray of a dolphin's flipper shows five rows of finger bones, wrist bones, two forearm bones and an upper arm bone, all wrapped inside a smooth paddle. A shark's fin, which does the same job, is stiffened by thin rods and contains none of those bones.
look.prompt: Why would a swimming animal have hand bones inside its flipper? What does the shark's fin tell you about the dolphin's ancestors?

check.q: A bat's wing and a human arm have the same bones in the same order. This makes them:
check.why: Same plan with different jobs is homology, a sign of shared ancestry.

check.q: Why are whale pelvic bones called vestigial?
choices: They are the whale's largest bones
They are leftovers from ancestors with hind legs
They help the whale swim faster
They are found only in baby whales
check.why: They serve no leg function today. They remain because whale ancestors walked on land.

check.q: Which pair shows analogous, not homologous, structures?
check.why: Bird and insect wings do the same job but are built on unrelated plans that evolved separately.

lessons.title: The Evidence in DNA
lessons.mainIdea: The more closely two species are related, the more similar their DNA, and shared broken genes show descent from the same ancestor.
reading: Darwin never saw a gene. If he had, he would have found his strongest evidence. Every living thing uses DNA, the same four bases, and almost the same codon table. That alone is hard to explain unless all life descends from one early ancestor. But the sequences say much more. When two species split from a shared ancestor, their DNA starts out alike and slowly gathers different mutations. The longer since the split, the more differences pile up.

So scientists can build family trees from DNA. Humans and chimpanzees differ in only about 1 to 2 percent of their aligned DNA. Humans and mice differ more; humans and fish more still. The trees built from DNA match, in almost every branch, the trees built from bones and fossils decades earlier. Two independent lines of evidence, one from rocks and one from molecules, agree. That agreement is what makes scientists confident.

The most telling evidence is in broken genes. Most mammals make their own vitamin C. Humans, chimpanzees and other primates cannot; we must eat it or get scurvy. The reason is a gene called GULO. Primates still carry it, but it is wrecked by mutations and no longer works. And the same wrecking mutations appear in the same spots in humans and chimps. A designer starting fresh would not include a broken gene. An ancestor that broke it and passed the ruin to all its descendants would.

DNA also records change within a species. Every person alive carries mutations that trace back through their mother's line and their father's line. By comparing them, scientists have traced human ancestry to Africa roughly 200,000 to 300,000 years ago, in agreement with the oldest Homo sapiens fossils, found in Morocco and Ethiopia.

words.d: an earlier species from which two or more later species descend
a gene that no longer works because of mutations, but is still carried in the DNA
the use of steady mutation buildup to estimate how long ago two species split

look.title: Two Essays With the Same Typo
look.text: Two students turn in essays. Both have the same sentence with the same misspelled word in the same place, and both have the same missing comma three lines later. The teacher does not need to see them copy to know one text came from the other.
look.prompt: How is a shared broken gene like a shared typo? Why is a shared error stronger evidence of common origin than a shared correct sentence?

check.q: Why does DNA similarity between two species tell you how closely they are related?
choices: All species started with different DNA
DNA changes only when a species goes extinct
Similar animals choose to swap genes
Mutations pile up steadily after two species split
check.why: Closely related species split recently and have had less time to gather different mutations.

check.q: Humans and chimpanzees both carry the GULO gene, broken in the same way. The best explanation is:
choices: Both inherited the broken gene from a shared ancestor
Chimpanzees caught the mutation from humans
Vitamin C damages the gene in primates
Both species broke it by chance in the same spots
check.why: Identical breaks in the same places are far too unlikely to happen twice by chance.

check.q: Trees of life built from fossils and from DNA mostly agree. Why does that matter?
choices: Two independent kinds of evidence point to the same history
It proves the trees were copied from each other
check.why: Agreement between independent methods is strong support that the shared history is real.

lessons.title: Darwin's Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Darwin proposed that living things change because individuals with helpful traits leave more offspring, so those traits spread through a population.
reading: In 1831 a young Charles Darwin boarded the ship HMS Beagle as its naturalist. For five years he collected plants, animals and fossils around the world. In the Galápagos Islands, off the coast of Ecuador, he collected small birds that he did not think much of at the time. Back in England, an expert told him they were all finches, different species on different islands, with beaks shaped for different foods. Darwin began to wonder whether one kind of finch had reached the islands and changed.

He also read the economist Thomas Malthus, who argued that people breed faster than food supplies grow. Darwin saw that this is true of every living thing. A pair of elephants, the slowest breeders known, could have millions of descendants in a few centuries if all survived. They do not. Most offspring die before they reproduce. Darwin asked: which ones survive? And he answered: on average, the ones best suited to their surroundings.

That is *natural selection*. Farmers already knew they could breed cattle for more milk or dogs for herding by choosing which animals to mate. Darwin argued that nature does the same, without any choosing. Individuals vary. Some variations help. Those individuals live longer and leave more young, who inherit the variation. Over many generations, the helpful variation becomes common. Given enough time, a population can change so much that it becomes a new species.

Darwin sat on the idea for 20 years, gathering evidence. In 1858 he received a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, working in what is now Indonesia, who had reached the same idea on his own. Their papers were read together at a meeting in London that July. Darwin's book, On the Origin of Species, appeared in November 1859 and sold out its first printing at once.

words.d: the process by which individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so the traits spread
the differences among individuals in a population
breeding in which people choose which individuals reproduce, as with crops and livestock

look.title: The Last Sentence of the Book
look.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, first edition, 1859
look.prompt: Darwin writes that forms 'are being' evolved, in the present tense. Why does he insist that evolution is still happening?

check.q: Which observation did Darwin take from Malthus?
choices: More offspring are born than can survive
check.why: Malthus wrote about human population outrunning food. Darwin saw it applies to all life.

check.q: How is natural selection like a farmer breeding cattle, and how is it different?
choices: Both involve choice by a person
Both change traits over generations, but in nature no one is choosing
check.why: Selection by survival and reproduction does the same work as a breeder's choice, with no breeder.

check.q: Why were Darwin's and Wallace's papers presented together in 1858?
choices: Wallace had reached the same idea independently
They worked in the same lab
check.why: Wallace's letter described natural selection on his own. Friends arranged a joint reading to credit both.

lessons.title: Four Conditions
lessons.mainIdea: Natural selection happens whenever there is variation, the variation is inherited, more are born than survive, and some variants survive better than others.
reading: Natural selection is not a mysterious force. It is what must happen when four ordinary conditions are met. First, individuals in a population *vary*. No two rabbits run at exactly the same speed. Second, some of that variation is *heritable*: it is passed from parent to offspring through genes. Third, more offspring are born than can possibly survive, so there is competition for food, space and mates. Fourth, individuals with some variations survive and reproduce more than others.

Put those together and the outcome is automatic. Faster rabbits escape foxes more often. They live to have more babies, who inherit faster legs. Each generation, the average rabbit is a little faster. No rabbit tried to become faster. No rabbit changed during its life. The population changed because the mix of alleles in it shifted. Individuals do not evolve; populations do.

A common mistake is to think that living things change because they need to. A giraffe does not grow a longer neck by stretching, and it cannot pass on a stretched neck. Selection can only work on variation that already exists, from mutation and the shuffling of meiosis. If no rabbit in a population carries an allele for faster legs, selection cannot make one. Mutation writes the options; selection picks among them.

Selection also has no goal. It does not aim for perfection or for humans. It only favors whatever works better right now, in this place. A trait that helps in a drought may hurt in a flood. That is why living things are full of compromises and leftover parts, and why they keep changing as their surroundings change.

words.d: able to be passed from parents to offspring through genes
all the members of one species living in one area
a heritable trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its surroundings

look.title: Salt Marsh Mice
look.text: A marsh floods every few years. Mice that happen to be slightly better swimmers survive the floods more often. Between floods, when the marsh is dry, being a good swimmer costs a little energy, and non-swimmers do slightly better.
look.prompt: What would you predict about swimming ability in this population after 50 years of frequent floods? After 50 dry years? Is either version of the mouse 'better'?

check.q: Which of the four conditions is missing if a trait cannot be passed to offspring?
check.why: Selection can only change a population if the favored trait is inherited by the next generation.

check.q: A student says giraffes got long necks by stretching for leaves and passing the stretch on. What is wrong?
choices: Giraffes have no variation in neck length
Stretching changes a body, not the genes that are inherited
check.why: Traits gained during life are not written into DNA. Selection acts on existing heritable variation.

check.q: Who or what evolves?
check.why: Individuals are born with their genes. It is the mix of alleles in the population that shifts.

lessons.title: Fitness and Adaptation
lessons.mainIdea: In biology, fitness means how many offspring an organism leaves, and an adaptation is any heritable trait that raises it.
reading: In everyday speech, the fittest is the strongest or the fastest. In biology, *fitness* means one thing only: how many offspring an individual leaves, compared with others in the population. A small, slow, well-camouflaged moth that has 200 babies is fitter than a big, strong one that is eaten before it breeds. Fitness is about reproduction, and survival only matters because you must survive long enough to reproduce.

An *adaptation* is a heritable trait that raises fitness in a particular place. The thick fur of an Arctic fox is an adaptation to cold. The long tongue of a hummingbird is an adaptation for reaching nectar. The bitter taste of some plants is an adaptation against being eaten. Adaptations look designed for their jobs because selection kept the versions that did the jobs best.

But adaptations fit the past, not the future. A trait is an adaptation only in the surroundings where it was selected. Move the Arctic fox to Texas and its fur becomes a burden. When surroundings change quickly, as when humans clear a forest or a new disease arrives, yesterday's adaptations may fail. Populations then either change fast enough, move, or die out.

Selection is not the only thing that shifts allele frequencies. In small populations, chance alone can change them; this is called genetic drift. A storm that kills half of a hundred beetles changes the mix of alleles for reasons that have nothing to do with fitness. Migration also matters: when individuals move between populations, they carry alleles with them. Evolution is the combined result of all these processes acting on the variation that mutation supplies.

words.d: how many offspring an individual leaves compared with others in its population
a change in allele frequencies caused by chance, strongest in small populations
the movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate and breed

look.title: Who Is Fitter?
look.text: Two male deer live in the same forest. One has huge antlers, wins every fight, and dies in his fourth winter from the cost of growing them, leaving three fawns. The other has small antlers, avoids fights, lives nine years, and leaves eleven fawns.
look.prompt: Which deer has higher fitness in the biological sense? Why might large antlers still be common in the population?

check.q: In biology, the 'fittest' individual is the one that:
check.why: Fitness is measured by reproductive success, not strength or lifespan alone.

check.q: Why can a trait that is an adaptation today become harmful later?
choices: Adaptations match past surroundings, which can change
check.why: Selection favored the trait in one setting. If the setting changes, the trait may no longer help.

check.q: A hurricane kills most of a tiny island's lizards at random. The alleles in the survivors differ from before. This is an example of:
check.why: The change was by chance, not because some alleles helped survival. That is drift.

lessons.title: Finches in a Drought
lessons.mainIdea: On one Galápagos island, a single drought shifted finch beak size in one generation, and scientists measured it happening.
reading: Darwin guessed that evolution was far too slow to see. He was wrong. In 1973 Peter and Rosemary Grant began catching, measuring and banding every medium ground finch on Daphne Major, a small volcanic island in the Galápagos. They measured wings, legs and, above all, beaks. Beak depth varied from bird to bird by a millimeter or so, and it was heritable: deep-beaked parents had deep-beaked chicks.

In 1977 the rains failed. Almost no seeds were produced. The finches ate through the small, soft seeds first. What remained were large, hard seeds that only a deep, strong beak could crack. The population fell from roughly 1,200 birds to fewer than 200. The survivors were not a random sample. On average, they had deeper beaks than the birds that died.

The next year the survivors bred, and their chicks had beaks measurably deeper than the generation before the drought, by roughly half a millimeter on average. That is natural selection, measured in the wild in a single year. Then in the 1980s came years of heavy rain and a flood of small seeds. Selection reversed, and beaks grew smaller again. The Grants have documented these swings for more than forty years.

Their work shows several things at once. Selection can be fast. It can go in either direction. It responds to conditions, not to a goal. And it requires variation that is already there: if every finch had the same beak, the drought would have killed at random and nothing would have shifted.

words.d: selection that favors one extreme of a trait, shifting the population's average
the top-to-bottom thickness of a bird's beak, a measure of its crushing strength
putting a numbered ring on a bird's leg so it can be tracked for life

look.title: Darwin on the Finches
look.text: In his account of the Beagle voyage, Darwin wrote that seeing such a range of beak shapes within one small, closely related group of birds, one might imagine that from an original scarcity of birds on the islands, a single species had been taken and modified for different purposes.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, Journal of Researches (Voyage of the Beagle), second edition, 1845 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Darwin wrote this before he had worked out natural selection. What was he already noticing, and what was he not yet able to explain?

check.q: Why did deep-beaked finches survive the 1977 drought better?
choices: They could fly to other islands
Only large, hard seeds were left, and deep beaks could crack them
check.why: Soft seeds ran out. Birds that could crack the hard seeds that remained had food.

check.q: What happened to average beak size when wet years brought many small seeds?
choices: It shifted back toward smaller beaks
check.why: With small seeds plentiful, smaller beaks did better. Selection reversed direction.

check.q: If every finch on the island had exactly the same beak depth, what would the drought have done to the average?
choices: Nothing, since there was no variation to select
check.why: Selection can only sort existing variation. With none, survival would be random with respect to beaks.

lessons.title: Moths, Bugs and Bacteria
lessons.mainIdea: Peppered moths, crop pests and disease bacteria all show populations changing fast under selection caused by humans.
reading: Before 1848 nearly every peppered moth in England was pale and speckled, which hid it on lichen-covered tree bark. That year a dark form was recorded near Manchester. As coal smoke killed the lichen and blackened the trees, dark moths became harder for birds to see, and pale ones easier. By 1895 about 98 percent of the moths around Manchester were dark. When clean-air laws cut the smoke in the second half of the twentieth century, the trees lightened and the pale form came back. Experiments releasing moths of both colors and watching birds hunt them confirmed the cause.

Farmers see the same thing. Spray a field with a pesticide and most insects die. But if a few carry a mutation that lets them survive, those few breed, and the next generation is full of resistant insects. This happened with DDT in the 1940s and 1950s and has happened with pesticide after pesticide since. In Illinois and Iowa, some western corn rootworms have evolved resistance to corn engineered to make its own insecticide. The spray did not create the resistance; it selected for it.

The most urgent case is *antibiotic resistance*. Bacteria divide every twenty minutes or so, so selection works on them at high speed. Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin, warned in 1945 that using too little of it could breed resistant germs. Today some infections resist nearly every antibiotic we have. Each time a person stops taking a prescription early or a farm feeds antibiotics to healthy animals, it is a selection experiment that the bacteria win.

These examples answer a common objection: that evolution has never been observed. It is observed constantly, wherever a population faces strong, steady selection. The lesson for medicine and farming is to change the selection: rotate drugs, use them only when needed, and plant refuges of unmodified crops so that susceptible insects survive to dilute the resistant ones.

words.d: the ability of bacteria to survive a drug that once killed them, spread by natural selection
the ability of insects or weeds to survive a chemical that once killed them
the spread of dark-colored forms of an animal in areas darkened by pollution

look.title: A Warning in 1945
look.text: In his Nobel lecture, Fleming cautioned that it was not hard to make microbes resistant to penicillin in the laboratory by exposing them to amounts too small to kill them, and that the same thing could happen in the body if people took too little of the drug.
look.prompt: Explain, using the four conditions of natural selection, why a dose too small to kill all the bacteria is exactly what breeds resistance.

check.q: Why did dark peppered moths become common near Manchester after 1848?
choices: Moths chose to become dark to hide
Birds ate more pale moths on darkened trees, so dark moths left more offspring
Dark moths were immune to pollution
check.why: Selection by bird predation favored whichever color was better hidden. On black bark, that was dark.

check.q: A pesticide stops working on a field's insects after ten years. What most likely happened?
choices: The insects mutated because they needed to
The insects learned to avoid it
Rare resistant insects survived and reproduced until most were resistant
check.why: Resistance alleles were already present in a few insects. Spraying killed the rest and selected for them.

check.q: Why does antibiotic resistance evolve especially fast?
choices: Bacteria have more DNA than humans
Bacteria can see the drug coming
check.why: Rapid reproduction means many generations, and many chances for selection, in a short time.

lessons.title: When Nothing Changes
lessons.mainIdea: The Hardy-Weinberg rule describes a population where allele frequencies stay constant, which lets scientists detect when evolution is happening.
reading: In 1908 a mathematician named Godfrey Hardy and a doctor named Wilhelm Weinberg separately answered a puzzle. If a dominant allele always shows, why does it not take over the population? Hardy showed with simple algebra that it does not. Left alone, allele frequencies stay the same generation after generation. Dominance changes how a trait looks, not how common the allele is.

Here is the idea. Call the frequency of one allele p and the other q, so that p + q = 1. If mating is random, the fraction of individuals with two copies of the first allele is p × p, the fraction with two copies of the second is q × q, and the fraction with one of each is 2 × p × q. If nothing disturbs the population, those fractions repeat every generation. This is the *Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium*.

The rule holds only if five things are true: no mutation, no migration in or out, a very large population, random mating, and no selection. Real populations rarely meet all five. That is the point. The rule describes what a population looks like when it is not evolving. When scientists count alleles in a real population and the numbers do not fit, something on the list is happening, and they can go looking for which one.

The rule also has a practical use. Suppose 1 person in 10,000 is born with a recessive genetic condition. That number is q × q, so q is 1 in 100. Then the carriers, 2 × p × q, are about 2 in 100, or 1 person in 50. A condition that seems rare can be carried by a surprising number of people who never show it.

words.d: the state of a population in which allele frequencies do not change from one generation to the next
how common one allele is among all the copies of a gene in a population
mating in which the choice of a partner does not depend on the trait being studied

look.title: One Gene, Two Alleles, No Selection
look.prompt: Check the numbers: does 49 + 42 + 9 equal 100? If a scientist found only 2 percent aa in this population, what might she conclude?

check.q: In a large population with random mating and no selection, what happens to a dominant allele's frequency over time?
choices: It rises until everyone has it
check.why: Hardy and Weinberg showed dominance does not change allele frequencies. Only the five disturbing forces do.

check.q: Why do scientists use a rule that real populations rarely obey?
choices: Because it is easy to memorize
Because deviations from it reveal that evolution is occurring
Because most populations obey it exactly
check.why: The rule is a baseline for no change. A mismatch points to selection, drift, migration or another cause.

check.q: A recessive condition appears in 1 of every 10,000 births. About how common are carriers?
check.why: q squared is 1/10,000, so q is 1/100. Carriers are 2pq, about 2/100, or 1 in 50.

lessons.title: How Species Form
lessons.mainIdea: A new species forms when two populations stop exchanging genes and drift apart until they can no longer interbreed.
reading: A *species* is a group of organisms that can breed with each other and produce fertile offspring. Horses and donkeys can mate, but their mules are sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species. The line is not always sharp, especially for bacteria and plants, but the idea works for most animals.

*Speciation* usually starts with a barrier. A river changes course and splits a population of mice. A few lizards raft on a log to an island. A mountain range rises. Once the two groups no longer exchange genes, they evolve separately. Different mutations appear on each side. Selection favors different traits in different places. Drift shifts allele frequencies at random. After enough generations, if the groups meet again, they may not recognize each other as mates, or their offspring may not survive.

The Galápagos finches are the textbook case. One ancestral finch reached the islands from the mainland. Different islands offered different foods, and populations on each island were selected for beaks suited to those foods. Today there are more than a dozen species, each adapted to a diet: seed-crushers, insect-eaters, cactus-flower feeders, even one that pecks at other birds and drinks their blood. This branching from one ancestor into many is called *adaptive radiation*.

Speciation does not always need a physical barrier. In the 1800s, in the Hudson River valley of New York, some apple maggot flies that had always laid eggs on hawthorn fruit began laying them on the newly planted apples. Apples ripen weeks earlier than hawthorns, so the two groups of flies now emerge at different times and rarely meet. Their genes are already diverging. It is speciation caught in the act, in an orchard.

words.d: a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring
the process by which one species splits into two
the rapid branching of one ancestral species into many, each adapted to a different way of life

look.title: Two Sides of a Canyon
look.text: Squirrels live on both rims of the Grand Canyon. The canyon opened millions of years ago, and squirrels do not cross it. On the north rim the squirrels have white tails and white bellies; on the south rim they have gray tails and dark bellies. They look like close relatives.
look.prompt: What happened to the gene flow between the two populations when the canyon opened? What would you need to test to decide whether they are now separate species?

check.q: Why are horses and donkeys considered separate species even though they can mate?
check.why: The definition requires fertile offspring. Sterile mules mean the two do not form one breeding population.

check.q: What usually happens first in speciation?
choices: The groups choose different foods on purpose
The two groups stop exchanging genes
A new species is born fully formed
check.why: Once gene flow stops, the populations gather different mutations and are selected in different ways.

check.q: The Galápagos finches are an example of adaptive radiation because:
choices: They all eat the same food
One ancestor gave rise to many species suited to different foods
They came from many different mainland species
check.why: A single colonizing species branched into many, each adapted to a different diet.

lessons.title: Extinction
lessons.mainIdea: Species go extinct constantly, and a few times in history most of life vanished at once, opening the way for survivors to diversify.
reading: More than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived are gone. *Extinction* is the normal end of a species, just as death is the normal end of an individual. Usually it is slow and local: surroundings change, a competitor arrives, a food source vanishes, and a species that cannot adapt or move dwindles to nothing. This steady loss is called background extinction.

A few times, the fossil record shows something else: a thin band of rock above which most species are simply missing. These are *mass extinctions*. Scientists count five major ones. The largest, about 252 million years ago, wiped out roughly nine of every ten marine species. The most famous, 66 million years ago, ended the non-bird dinosaurs. In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez found that the rock layer from that moment, all over the world, is rich in iridium, an element rare on Earth but common in asteroids. A crater of the right age, about 150 kilometers wide, was later identified near Chicxulub, Mexico.

Mass extinctions clear the stage. For 150 million years, mammals lived in the shadow of dinosaurs, most of them no bigger than a cat. Within a few million years of the asteroid, mammals had radiated into whales, bats, horses and primates. The survivors of a catastrophe are not necessarily the best adapted; they may simply be small, or able to burrow, or lucky. What they inherit is an emptied world.

Extinctions caused by people are recorded in living memory. The passenger pigeon once flew over Illinois in flocks that darkened the sky for hours; the last one, named Martha, died in the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Many biologists argue that the current rate of extinction, driven by habitat loss, hunting and climate change, is far above the background rate. Whether it becomes a sixth mass extinction depends on choices being made now.

words.d: the permanent disappearance of a species
an event in which a large fraction of all species die out in a short time
a metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, found in the rock layer from 66 million years ago

look.title: The Thin Gray Line
look.text: In a road cut in Italy, a geologist points to a layer of clay about a centimeter thick. Below it, the limestone is full of tiny fossil shells of many kinds. Above it, the same limestone holds only a few kinds, and they are much smaller. Chemical tests show the clay is rich in iridium.
look.prompt: What two separate observations here point to a sudden catastrophe? Why was the iridium so important to the explanation?

check.q: What evidence linked the extinction of the dinosaurs to an asteroid?
choices: A written record from early humans
Dinosaur bones found in a crater
A worldwide rock layer rich in iridium from that time
check.why: Iridium is rare on Earth and common in asteroids. Its worldwide spike marked the impact.

check.q: How did the extinction of the dinosaurs affect mammals?
choices: Mammals diversified into many new forms once the dinosaurs were gone
check.why: With the dominant animals gone, mammals radiated into the empty roles.

check.q: Which best describes background extinction?
choices: The sudden loss of most species at once
The slow, steady loss of species over normal time
The extinction of individuals within a species
check.why: Background extinction is the ordinary, ongoing rate, unlike the spikes of mass extinctions.

lessons.title: The Tree of Life
lessons.mainIdea: All living things can be arranged on one branching tree of descent, and DNA has redrawn its deepest branches.
reading: In 1837, two years after visiting the Galápagos, Darwin sketched a branching diagram in a notebook. Above it he wrote two words: 'I think.' The sketch showed species splitting from common ancestors like the limbs of a tree. Before Darwin, naturalists like Carl Linnaeus had grouped living things by similarity, in nested boxes. Species sat inside genera, genera inside families, and so on. Darwin explained why the boxes nest. Similar species share a recent ancestor. The bigger boxes share older ones.

A diagram of these relationships is a *phylogenetic tree*. Each branch point is a common ancestor. Two species that join at a recent branch point are close relatives. Reading the tree, you find surprises. Birds are a branch of the dinosaurs. Whales are a branch of the hoofed mammals. Fungi are closer to animals than to plants. The tree is a hypothesis. It is tested every time a new fossil or genome is compared with it.

The deepest branches were redrawn in 1977. Carl Woese compared the RNA of ribosomes across many organisms. He found that some microbes, then lumped in with bacteria, were as different from bacteria as bacteria are from us. He named them *Archaea*. Life, it turned out, has three main *domains*: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. The last includes every plant, animal, fungus and protist. Humans are one twig on the eukaryote branch.

At the root of the tree is a single ancestor. All living things descend from it, starting roughly 3.5 to 4 billion years ago. The evidence is the shared machinery: the same DNA, the same code, the same ribosomes, the same basic energy chemistry in every cell. Look at a redwood, a mushroom, a bacterium in your gut, or your own hand. You are looking at branches of one tree.

words.d: a branching diagram that shows how species are related by descent
one of the three largest groups of life: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya
a domain of single-celled microbes that differ from bacteria as much as bacteria differ from us
the science of naming and grouping living things

look.title: Two Words Above a Sketch
look.text: Above a sketch of a trunk splitting into branches, with letters at the tips standing for species, Darwin wrote just two words: I think.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, Notebook B, 1837 (description of the page)
look.prompt: Darwin drew the tree 22 years before publishing. What might he have needed to gather before he was willing to say more than 'I think'?

check.q: On a phylogenetic tree, what does a branch point stand for?
choices: A common ancestor of the branches above it
check.why: Each split marks the ancestor from which the branches beyond it descend.

check.q: What did Carl Woese discover by comparing ribosomal RNA?
choices: That DNA is a double helix
That plants are closer to animals than to fungi
That Archaea are a separate domain of life
check.why: Archaea had been mistaken for bacteria. Their RNA showed a deep, separate branch.

check.q: Which is the strongest evidence that all living things share one ancestor?
choices: All use the same DNA, genetic code and ribosomes
All organisms are about the same size
check.why: Shared molecular machinery across every domain is best explained by inheritance from one root.

review.q: The team that found Tiktaalik chose Ellesmere Island because:
choices: Fossils are always found near the poles
Rocks of the predicted age and type were exposed there
It was the closest site to their university
review.why: They predicted a fish-to-land transition in 375-million-year-old freshwater rocks and looked where such rocks lay open.

review.q: A whale's flipper contains finger bones. This is best explained by:
review.why: The bones are homologous with land mammals' limbs, inherited from a common ancestor.

review.q: Which condition is NOT required for natural selection?
review.why: Selection has no goal and needs no intent. It only needs heritable variation and unequal reproduction.

review.q: During the 1977 drought, finches with deeper beaks survived because:
choices: Deep beaks are more attractive to mates
review.why: Soft seeds vanished. Deep beaks could crack the hard seeds that were left.

review.q: Why does a population that does not fit Hardy-Weinberg numbers interest scientists?
choices: It means the math is wrong
It means something is changing allele frequencies
It means the population is extinct
It means all mating is random
review.why: The rule is the baseline for no change. A mismatch signals selection, drift, migration or mutation.

review.q: The dark form of the peppered moth declined after clean-air laws because:
choices: Pale moths were once again better hidden on lighter trees
review.why: With soot gone, bark lightened and pale moths regained the camouflage advantage.

review.q: What does the iridium layer found around the world mark?
choices: An asteroid impact 66 million years ago
review.why: Iridium is rare on Earth but common in asteroids. Its worldwide spike dates the impact.

review.q: Humans and chimpanzees share the same broken vitamin C gene. What does this show?
choices: Both inherited the broken gene from a common ancestor
The gene was broken by the same diet
Both species need no vitamin C
review.why: Identical breaks in the same places are the mark of a shared ancestor that passed the ruin to both.
